parsed.explanation: The combined regime is severe for a trans visitor. National document rules allow refusal and possible lifetime ineligibility where sex is doubted, and custody records document abuse and forced conversion practices. The division adds a universal facility ban in publicly owned buildings including airports, enforced by private bounty suits and civil/criminal penalties, plus invalidation of state IDs. A pending lawsuit, state anti-discrimination law and national hate-crime coverage are not shown to have stopped the facility or ID provisions. The result is below the 0.25 anchor but above the 0.15 anchors because execution and routine arrest for presentation are not documented.

entry_documents.exposure: National rules require birth-sex markers for new passports, stop new X markers, and direct posts to refuse visa cases with sex discrepancies and consider fraud-based permanent ineligibility; trans travelers report confiscation or stranding.
entry_documents.protection: Existing X-marker passports remain valid until expiry; a fraud finding is not automatic and requires four elements with limited waivers; litigation is pending.
entry_documents.interaction: A visitor using a home passport with an X or altered marker can face refusal, secondary screening or a lifetime bar; division ID invalidation adds domestic credential conflict but the visitor primarily carries foreign documents.

investigation_detention_custody.exposure: National immigration custody is documented as subjecting trans men to forced labour, beatings, solitary confinement and sexual abuse; national corrections policies mandate hair cutting, hormone removal and psychiatric substitution for trans inmates.
investigation_detention_custody.protection: National hate-crime law covers gender identity, and some executive orders are enjoined, but no custody-specific protection for trans visitors is documented.
investigation_detention_custody.interaction: A border discrepancy or facility incident that leads to detention routes the visitor into a system with documented severe abuse and no effective visitor remedy.

federal_state_facilities.exposure: The division confines trans people to birth-sex facilities in all publicly owned buildings including airports, schools and government offices; it imposes civil/criminal penalties up to $1,000 and authorises private bounty suits of at least $1,000.
federal_state_facilities.protection: The division has prohibited gender-identity discrimination in public accommodations since 2020, and a civil-liberties lawsuit challenges the new law, but no injunction or ruling is recorded.
federal_state_facilities.interaction: Because airports are public buildings, a trans visitor using a restroom during transit is exposed to bounty suits and penalties regardless of local agency enforcement; the law reaches visitors on interstate travel.

care_services.exposure: National policy treats gender-affirming care for minors as harmful and proposes insurance bars; the division bans care for minors, though a May 2026 injunction blocks enforcement. Custody denies hormones.
care_services.protection: The division injunction protects minor care pending trial; state anti-discrimination law does not clearly reach trans-specific care denial by providers.
care_services.interaction: Adult visitor routine care is not documented as restricted; a travelling family with a trans minor faces care bans, school-transition prosecution climate and document conflicts.

threat_framing_law_enforcement.exposure: The national counterterrorism strategy prioritises neutralising groups described as radically pro-transgender; a justice-department reward memo mentions radical gender ideology, though not as a reward criterion; schools face investigation for gender ideology.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.protection: The strategy states counterterrorism powers will not target mere disagreement, and several related orders are enjoined.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.interaction: This raises risk mainly for visible activism or advocacy, not ordinary sightseeing, but it colours official response if a visitor is detained or reports a crime.

minors_guardians.exposure: The division facility law reaches schools and public buildings and applies to minors; national policy directs prosecution of teachers who use preferred names or facilitate social transition; care for minors is banned nationally in many states.
minors_guardians.protection: The division minor care ban is temporarily enjoined; parental lawsuit is active; national hate-crime law covers gender identity.
minors_guardians.interaction: A trans minor with a guardian using an airport or other public building is exposed to the facility ban and bounty; school-related measures mainly affect residents, but the family climate is hostile.

street_violence_police_response.exposure: The division hate-crime law omits gender identity; only national law covers it. Official advisories warn trans travelers, and the division is rated Do Not Travel by a trans legal-risk assessment.
street_violence_police_response.protection: National hate-crime statute covers gender identity; the division has public-accommodations protections since 2020; no visitor-specific police response data is recorded.
street_violence_police_response.interaction: A victim may rely on national hate-crime coverage, but local charging practice for gender-identity bias is undocumented; the division statutory gap weakens local recourse.

remedies_unknowns.exposure: The division bounty is enforced by private persons, not agency or prosecutor discretion; ID invalidation notices have no grace period and reissue is at the holder’s expense; criminal/civil penalties attach to facility use.
remedies_unknowns.protection: Civil-liberties litigation, the state public-accommodations law, national hate-crime coverage and court injunctions exist, but none is shown to have stopped the facility or ID provisions.
remedies_unknowns.interaction: Remedies are pending and uncertain, while the bounty mechanism operates independently; enforcement counts for suits and invalidations are not documented.

anchor_checks.comparison: Vellandra uses border denial and removal without arrest. This regime is lower because, beyond border refusal and lifetime ineligibility, it adds universal facility penalties and private bounty suits in airports plus documented custody abuse.

Meridia documents police extortion, document confiscation and overnight cells. This regime lacks documented routine street shakedowns but has a broader statutory facility bounty reaching airports and a national fraud-based lifetime entry bar, so it sits slightly lower.

Varnalia documents routine arrests for presentation, months of pretrial custody, beatings and a capital provision. This regime has no comparable routine arrest for presentation or capital execution, so it is higher, though custody abuse and universal facility exposure remain severe.

Kestrel Isles uses extended secondary screening and discretionary refusal but keeps penalties administrative. This regime is lower because it combines entry refusal with criminal/civil facility penalties, private bounty suits and documented abusive custody.

parsed.synthesis: The parent regime supplies the entry-document exposure: new passports and visas follow birth sex, discrepant cases can be refused, and fraud findings can produce lifetime ineligibility. The division supplies the sharpest universal exposure: birth-sex facility rules in all public buildings, including airports, enforced by private bounty suits and penalties, alongside invalidated state IDs. A visitor using a foreign passport still meets the division’s public-building rules during transit. Detention, if triggered, enters a custody system with documented abuse. Pending litigation and partial anti-discrimination law are real but not shown to operate against the facility and ID provisions, so they do not offset the combined exposure.
